misconception.description: adding cash flows from different years together before discounting, so money that has not arrived yet is valued as though it had

worked_example.text: A bakery is offered an oven costing EUR 25,000 today that would save EUR 18,000 of cash at the end of each of the next two years. The bakery requires a 20% return.
worked_example.solution: Year 1: 18,000 / 1.2 = EUR 15,000. Year 2: 18,000 / 1.44 = EUR 12,500. The savings are worth EUR 27,500 today, so the NPV is 27,500 - 25,000 = EUR 2,500 and the oven is worth buying.

problem.text: A cafe can buy a coffee machine for EUR 50,000 today. It would save EUR 36,000 of cash at the end of year 1 and EUR 36,000 at the end of year 2. The cafe requires a 20% return a year. What is the net present value of the purchase?

distractors.note: the documented misconception: the two years added together with no discounting
discounting the total once instead of each year by its own factor

hints: The two savings arrive at different times, so they are not worth the same today and cannot be added together as they stand. Deal with each year on its own first.
Money arriving in one year is divided by one plus the required return. Money arriving in two years has waited twice as long, so the divisor is squared.
Add the two present values, then subtract what the cafe pays today. What is left is the net present value.
worked_solution: Step 1: discount year 1: 36,000 / 1.2 = EUR 30,000. Step 2: discount year 2 by two years of waiting: 36,000 / 1.44 = EUR 25,000. Step 3: the savings are worth 30,000 + 25,000 = EUR 55,000 in today's money. Step 4: subtract the price paid now: 55,000 - 50,000 = EUR 5,000. The NPV is positive, so the machine earns more than the 20% the cafe requires. Adding the raw savings instead would give 72,000 - 50,000 = EUR 22,000 and would treat money that has not arrived as though it were already in the till.

near_transfer.text: The same coffee machine, costing EUR 50,000 today and saving EUR 36,000 at the end of year 1 and EUR 36,000 at the end of year 2, is reassessed as much riskier and the required return is raised to 50% a year. What is its net present value now?

distractors.note: the misconception: with no discounting the rate change makes no difference at all
discounting the total by a single year

far_transfer.text: A maintenance contract will pay its holder EUR 20,000 at the end of next year and EUR 20,000 at the end of the year after. An investor requires a 25% annual return. What is the most the investor should pay for it today?

distractors.note: the misconception: paying the undiscounted total of what will be received
discounting both receipts by one year only
